messages.author: 7085c26ce2c85a37
messages.subject: ez question
parts:
hi,
I'm trying to plot model predictions and estimated confidence
intervals of a mixed-effects model with a single fixed effect and two
random effects + random slopes:

The model (using lme4) looks like this:
model<-lmer(dv~condition+(1+condition|item)+(1+condition|
participant),data=data)

How can I do this using the ez package?
Maybe this is trivial, but I don't see how.

Michael.

messages.author: cb25d91fd630a4e5
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] ez question
parts:
Check out ezPredict & ezPlot2 from the dev version
(http://github.com/mike-lawrence/ez) of ez. I've never tried ezPredict
with multiple random effects, but give this a try:

preds = ezPredict(
fit = model
, effect_variability_only = FALSE
)
p = ezPlot2(
predictions = preds
, x = .(condition)
, x_lab = 'Condition'
)
print(p$plot)

Note that p$plot is a modifiable ggplot2 object. Also note that in the
call to ezPredict above I set the "effect_variability_only" argument
to FALSE. By default this value is TRUE, but I should probably change
that. If you have your variables set up with contrasts that make them
independent of the intercept, then "effect_variability_only=TRUE" will
remove the intercept variance, solving the age-old issue of presenting
inferentially useful CIs when plotting raw values. However, if you
don't have your variables set up with proper contrasts before doing
the model, "effect_variability_only=TRUE" can lead to strange looking
results (e.g. one level of your variables will have a CI of zero
width).

Mike

messages.author: cb25d91fd630a4e5
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] Re: ez question
parts:
When "effect_variability_only = FALSE", the CI's include all fixed
effects variances/covariances from the model, including the intercept,
so: (1) you can't just compare each CI to the first level's mean (even
when using "treatment contrasts"); and (2) comparing pairs of points
by looking at the overlap of their CIs will be conservative.

So, when you are interested in post-hoc comparisons, it is best to set
up your variable with theoretically interesting contrasts that don't
confound a level with the intercept, compute the model, then compute
ezPredict predictions using "effect_variability_only = TRUE", after
which the CIs from ezPlot2 will be useful for comparing points.
Remember, with 95% CIs: if they fail to overlap, they're "different",
if they overlap each-others' means, they're "non-different", but if
they overlap a bit, it's probably a good idea to look at the
difference score CI to see what the story is. If you have only two
levels in the variable you wish to collapse to a difference score, you
can just use the "diff" argument to ezPlot2. However, if you have 3+
levels, you'll need to subset the predictions before using ezPlot2, as
in:

#subset to compare just None & Center
preds2 = list(
cells = preds$cells[preds$cells$cue %in% c('None','Center'),]
, boots = preds$boots[preds$boots$cue %in% c('None','Center'),]
)
p = ezPlot2(
predictions = preds2
, diff = .(cue)
, do_plot = FALSE
)
print(p$cells)
print(p$boot_stats)

(Note that regardless of what contrasts are used and whether you set
"effect_variability_only" to true or false, the difference scores
computed as above will come out the same; the benefit of using proper
contrasts and setting "effect_variability_only" to true is that in
some cases you can get away without needing to compute the difference
score.)
